task: 5.1.7 If SQLite still misses accepted analytical budget after evidence-backed tuning, conduct architecture review through GraphAnalyticsPort; do not add distributed/authoritative backend or ANN scope without replacement decision.

conditional_trigger.condition: SQLite still misses accepted analytical budget after evidence-backed tuning
conditional_trigger.evidence: performance/samples.json: control_center_search idle p95=427.111ms vs threshold=250ms — Fail
conditional_trigger.prior_tuning_outcome: tuning-report.json: all 7 tuning areas verified correct within hard limits; no code changes made; future_opportunities identified frontier-level BFS batching as the sole remaining optimization

budget_miss.variance_note: Extremely tight CI (±2.4ms around mean). The miss is structural, not measurement noise. The 30 warm samples span [404ms, 431ms] — every single sample exceeds the 250ms threshold with no outlier explanation.

control_center_search_pipeline: 1. FTS5 full-corpus search on 100k search_documents → returns top-5 seeds by BM25
3. Graph BFS from 5 FTS5 seeds through 256k link records (batch_read_edges per node)
4. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) merge of FTS5 and graph candidates
5. Truth/policy gate + diversity cap + marginal-utility token packing

component_timing_estimate.method: Indirect — measured via one_hop_neighborhood and core_retrieval as isolated probes
component_timing_estimate.graph_bfs_estimate_ms: ~330ms (one_hop_neighborhood idle p95=334.887ms; same BFS path, 1-hop only)
component_timing_estimate.conclusion: The graph BFS accounts for approximately 76% of the control_center_search total latency (~330ms out of ~430ms). FTS5 contributes ~23%. The remaining ~1% is classifier, RRF, and packing.

root_cause_analysis.primary_bottleneck: Graph BFS: bounded N+1 SQL query pattern — batch_read_edges() is called once per node rather than once per hop-frontier

pattern_description.current: BFS while-loop pops one node at a time from the queue, calls batch_read_edges(conn, &[current_id.clone()], req) with a single-element slice per iteration, then calls is_entity_authorized() and node_has_hidden_edges() per neighbour.

sql_calls_per_bfs_worst_case.batch_read_edges_calls: up to 120 (one per node, MAX_NODES_HARD cap)
sql_calls_per_bfs_worst_case.total_sql_statements_for_5_seeds: 5 seed expansions × ~3 calls/node × ~24 nodes/seed = ~360 SQL statements for a typical 3-hop traversal
sql_calls_per_bfs_worst_case.note: batch_read_edges() already accepts &[String] (batched IN-clause API). Only the BFS caller passes a 1-element slice.

pattern_description.why_it_is_slow_at_100k_scale: Each batch_read_edges call issues a parameterized SELECT against relationships_v2 (256,117 rows) with a LEFT JOIN to evidence_v2. Even with the composite policy index (idx_relationships_v2_policy), each call requires an index seek + evidence join + GROUP BY. At 120 such calls the accumulated latency is ~330ms on the reference hardware (confirmed by one_hop_neighborhood measurement).

root_cause_analysis.secondary_contributor: FTS5 full-corpus search over 100k documents contributes ~98ms (core_retrieval p95). This is below its own 120ms threshold and is not a blocker, but it adds ~23% to the combined total.
dismissed_causes: Index coverage: all 8 hot-path queries verified index-backed (query-plans.json). The relationships_v2 policy composite index is used on every batch_read_edges call. Not a root cause.
Worker concurrency: correctly bounded (DEFAULT_MAX_WORKERS=4, pressure policy halves under load). Not a root cause.
Prepared statements: prepare() vs prepare_cached() overhead is negligible at this call frequency. Not a root cause.
Revision cache: graph_revision fetched at most once per operation, not per node. Not a root cause.
Memory/paging: measurement was 'warm idle' with in-memory SQLite (100k records fully in RAM). OS page cache effects do not explain the miss.
Hardware anomaly: 30 samples show variance of only ±13ms with no thermal spike or outlier. Measurement is stable.

graph_analytics_port_evaluation.definition_source: architecture.md §Evolution Seams: 'Stable seams are canonical v2 DTOs, GraphQueryPort, GraphAnalyticsPort, VectorStorePort, relation registry versions, model manifests, schema migrations, and Interchange v1. They do not introduce multi-user, multi-device, consensus, or a second authority.'
graph_analytics_port_evaluation.implementation_status: Not yet implemented. No Rust trait, struct, or module named GraphAnalyticsPort exists in the repository. It is a named evolution seam reserved in the architecture document for future isolation — a planned boundary, not a deployed one.
graph_analytics_port_evaluation.intended_role: GraphAnalyticsPort is the seam at which the graph read service (memory::graph) can be backed by a different engine without changing the retrieval or cognition layers. Its contract would minimally include: bounded BFS traversal, policy-first filtering, revision-pinned snapshots, and hop/node/edge hard caps. The concrete SQLite implementation (expand_graph_bfs_inner) lives behind this seam.

relevance_to_current_miss.isolation_value: Extracting a GraphAnalyticsPort trait would allow the BFS implementation to be swapped. However, the bottleneck is not the backend engine choice — it is the per-node SQL call pattern inside the existing SQLite implementation. A port boundary does not change how many SQL statements are issued within the implementation behind the port.
relevance_to_current_miss.conclusion: Introducing GraphAnalyticsPort as a trait boundary now would be a valid architectural cleanup but would NOT reduce the 427ms latency by itself. The optimization opportunity (frontier-level batching) is a change to the algorithm inside the existing SQLite BFS implementation, not a backend replacement.

when_graphanalyticsport_becomes_actionab: If frontier-level batching is applied and the threshold is still missed, and an alternative graph engine is under evaluation.
As a cleanup step when implementing the frontier-level batching refactor, to isolate the BFS contract before restructuring the loop.

As a prerequisite before any future engine evaluation — architecture.md requires any future derived backend to 'first fail optimized 100k budgets, rebuild from SQLite, consume revisions, enforce policy, and preserve contracts'.

frontier_level_batching_opportunity.description: Refactor expand_graph_bfs_inner to collect a complete hop-frontier (all nodes at depth D) before issuing SQL, then call batch_read_edges() once per hop with all frontier node IDs in a single IN-clause. Optionally batch is_entity_authorized() and node_has_hidden_edges() similarly.
frontier_level_batching_opportunity.current_complexity: O(nodes) SQL calls — up to 120 batch_read_edges + 120 is_entity_authorized + 120 node_has_hidden_edges = up to 360 SQL statements
frontier_level_batching_opportunity.proposed_complexity: O(hops) SQL calls — 3 batch_read_edges (one per hop depth) + 1 batched is_entity_authorized + 1 batched node_has_hidden_edges = 5 SQL statements
frontier_level_batching_opportunity.reduction_factor: Up to 72× fewer SQL statements (360 → 5 in worst case)

feasibility.api_readiness: batch_read_edges() already accepts &[String] — the batched IN-clause is already implemented. Only the BFS loop caller needs to be restructured.
correctness_invariants_preserved: Policy filtering (namespace/scope/sensitivity) is enforced inside batch_read_edges SQL — still applied to every edge
Visited/path guards remain in the BFS state; frontier collection does not change cycle safety
Deadline check (req.deadline.is_expired()) is evaluated once per frontier collection rather than once per node — still bounded
Authorization (is_entity_authorized) must be batched carefully: need one SQL query with IN-clause over all frontier neighbours rather than per-node; same policy correctness applies
feasibility.implementation_scope: Localized to expand_graph_bfs_inner in graph_strategy.rs. No schema change, no new authority, no new port required. Affects only the BFS loop structure.
feasibility.estimated_latency_after_refactor: If 360 SQL calls at ~0.9ms each = ~330ms collapses to ~5 SQL calls at ~15ms each (larger IN-clause) = ~75ms, the graph BFS contribution would drop from ~330ms to ~75ms. Combined with FTS5 (~98ms) and overhead (~5ms), projected control_center_search total: ~178ms vs 250ms threshold — Pass with ~72ms margin.
feasibility.note: The 15ms-per-batched-call estimate is conservative; a single IN-clause over all frontier nodes in one SQL statement against the indexed relationships_v2 is likely faster than 120 sequential single-node queries. Actual reduction may be larger.

rationale: The architecture review identifies a concrete, bounded, in-place fix (frontier-level BFS batching) that is projected to bring control_center_search latency from ~427ms to ~178ms — within the 250ms threshold with margin.

The fix requires no schema change, no new authority store, no new engine, no new port boundary, and no architectural replacement. It is a refactor of a single function's loop structure using an API (batch_read_edges) that already exists.

No replacement of the SQLite backend is warranted. SQLite handles this workload correctly once the per-node SQL anti-pattern is removed. The 256k-row relationships_v2 table with the composite policy index is sufficient — the bottleneck was call frequency, not engine capability.

GraphAnalyticsPort does not need to be introduced as a prerequisite for this fix. It remains a valid future evolution seam for backend isolation but is not required to resolve the current performance miss.
The non-negotiable constraints from the spec are fully preserved: no distributed/authoritative backend, no ANN/HNSW scope, one SQLite authority.
replacement_decision.recommended_action: Implement frontier-level BFS batching in expand_graph_bfs_inner. Collect the full hop-frontier before calling batch_read_edges(). Batch is_entity_authorized() and node_has_hidden_edges() similarly. Rerun V-PERF-01 control_center_search after the fix to confirm threshold passage.
replacement_decision.architectural_change_prohibited_without: A replacement decision would only be required if: (a) frontier-level batching is applied and V-PERF-01 still fails, AND (b) no further in-place SQL optimization exists, AND (c) a specific alternative engine (e.g., a specialized graph index) is evaluated against the architecture.md requirements: rebuild from SQLite, consume revisions, enforce policy, preserve contracts, fail 100k budgets first.

summary.miss_detail: control_center_search idle p95=427ms vs 250ms threshold — 177ms over budget (70.8% overage)
summary.root_cause: Bounded N+1 SQL pattern in expand_graph_bfs_inner: batch_read_edges called once per node (up to 120 calls) instead of once per hop-frontier (3 calls). The batch API already exists; only the BFS loop needs restructuring.
summary.graph_analytics_port_status: Named evolution seam in architecture.md; not yet implemented as a Rust trait. Not required to resolve the current miss. Remains a valid future isolation boundary.
summary.fix_description: Frontier-level BFS batching in graph_strategy.rs::expand_graph_bfs_inner — collect full hop-frontier before SQL, issue O(3) batch_read_edges calls instead of O(120)
summary.next_action: Implement frontier-level BFS batching; rerun V-PERF-01

reviewer.verdict: Pass — architecture review complete; fix path identified within existing architecture; no replacement decision required; no non-negotiable violated
